subject: Computer Networking
title: How Wi-Fi Works
description: A short lesson to help you apply How Wi-Fi Works.

hook.text: You connect to Wi-Fi and browse instantly. Behind the scenes, your device and the router just ran a complex protocol.

buildup.text: Wi-Fi uses the 802.11 standard. Your device scans for networks, picks one, authenticates, and starts exchanging frames.

discovery.text: All devices on the same channel share airtime. Wi-Fi uses collision avoidance — listen before you talk.

twist.text: Unlike Ethernet, Wi-Fi is half-duplex. A device can't send and receive at the same time on the same channel.

climax.text: Despite these limitations, Wi-Fi 6E delivers multi-gigabit speeds. Smart engineering overcomes physical constraints.

punchline.text: Wi-Fi is Ethernet without wires — and with more challenges.

quiz.question: Why can't Wi-Fi devices send and receive simultaneously?
options: Wi-Fi is half-duplex on each channel
Routers can only handle one device at a time

details.summary: Wi-Fi uses radio waves in unlicensed spectrum bands to create local area wireless networks. An access point broadcasts a network name and devices associate with it after authentication. Data is transmitted using OFDM modulation with CSMA/CA to manage channel access among multiple devices.
details.whyItMatters: Wi-Fi is the most widely used wireless networking technology, connecting billions of devices in homes, offices, and public spaces. Understanding how it works helps troubleshoot and optimize wireless networks.
takeaways: Wi-Fi uses 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and 6 GHz unlicensed frequency bands
CSMA/CA prevents devices from transmitting simultaneously
Access points bridge wireless clients to the wired network

faq.question: What is the difference between 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz Wi-Fi?
faq.answer: The 2.4 GHz band has longer range and better wall penetration but only three non-overlapping channels and heavy congestion from many devices. The 5 GHz band offers more channels, less interference, and faster speeds but shorter range. Most routers use both simultaneously in dual-band mode.

faq.question: How does Wi-Fi share the channel among devices?
faq.answer: Wi-Fi uses CSMA/CA — devices listen before transmitting and back off if the channel is busy. Only one device transmits at a time on a channel, taking turns in millisecond intervals. More devices means more waiting. MU-MIMO in modern Wi-Fi allows simultaneous transmission to multiple devices.
